text:
The question of whether we have a duty to ourselves—and whether self-harm constitutes a moral wrong—is one of the oldest and most contentious in ethics. I will argue that **yes, we do have a duty to oneself**, and that even in the absence of dependents, a person who harms only themselves has done something morally wrong. This position rests on three pillars: the intrinsic value of the person, the coherence of self-regarding duties, and the social nature of human flourishing.

**First, the duty to oneself is grounded in the intrinsic worth of the individual.** Immanuel Kant famously argued that rational beings are ends in themselves, never merely means. This principle applies not only to how we treat others but also to how we treat ourselves. To harm oneself—whether through reckless self-destruction, chronic neglect, or the deliberate suppression of one’s own capacities—is to treat one’s own rational nature as a mere tool for momentary gratification or escape. For example, a person who abuses drugs to the point of permanent cognitive damage is not just “choosing their own path”; they are degrading the very faculty (reason) that gives their choices moral weight. Even if no one else suffers, the act violates the respect owed to the rational agent that the person *is*. Thus, self-harm is a contradiction: the self that wills the harm is the same self that is harmed, and in doing so, it undermines the ground of its own moral standing.

**Second, the concept of a duty to oneself is logically coherent and morally necessary.** Some philosophers, like John Stuart Mill, have argued that we cannot have duties to ourselves because we can simply release ourselves from any obligation—duties require a claimant who can demand performance. But this objection fails. A duty to oneself is not like a contract between two parties; it is more like a duty to uphold a standard of excellence. Consider the duty to keep promises. If I promise a friend to meet them, I have a duty to them. But if I make a private resolution to learn a language, do I have no duty to keep it? I would argue that I do—not because someone else will be disappointed, but because the act of making a commitment to oneself is an exercise of self-respect and integrity. Breaking that commitment without good reason is a form of self-betrayal, a failure to honor the rational project of one’s own life. Moreover, without a duty to oneself, we would have no basis for duties to others in many cases. For instance, if I have no duty to preserve my own health, then I cannot be blamed for becoming a burden on others due to preventable illness—but that blame only makes sense if I first owed it to myself to stay well. Thus, self-regarding duties are the foundation of other-regarding duties, not a contradiction.

**Third, even in the absence of dependents, self-harm is socially and existentially wrong because it violates the relational nature of human life.** Humans are not isolated atoms; we are inherently social beings whose identities are formed in community. Even a hermit who harms only himself still lives in a world shaped by others—he uses language, tools, and knowledge passed down from generations. To harm oneself is to damage a node in the web of human culture and potential. For example, a brilliant scientist who, out of despair, destroys her own mental faculties through self-neglect is not merely hurting herself; she is depriving humanity of future discoveries, even if she has no current dependents. More fundamentally, the existentialist insight is that we are “beings-toward-death” who must create meaning. To harm oneself is to reject the project of meaning-making itself, which is a betrayal of the human capacity for freedom and creativity. Even if no one else knows or cares, the act diminishes the sum of human flourishing—because the person’s own flourishing is part of that sum.

**Objections and responses.** A common objection is that a person has the right to do what they want with their own body and life, as long as they don’t harm others. This is the liberal harm principle. But this objection conflates *liberty* with *moral permissibility*. We may have a legal right to self-harm (e.g., smoking, extreme sports), but that does not mean it is morally neutral. Legal rights protect against state coercion, not against moral judgment. Another objection is that “harm” is subjective—what one person calls harm, another calls growth (e.g., fasting, asceticism). I agree that not all self-denial is harmful; the duty is to preserve and develop one’s rational and moral capacities, not to avoid all discomfort. The wrong arises when the harm is *disproportionate* or *destructive of one’s agency*—e.g., addiction, suicide, or chronic self-deception. These are not mere lifestyle choices; they are attacks on the very conditions of moral agency.

**Conclusion.** Therefore, a duty to oneself is real, and self-harm is wrong even without dependents. The wrong is not that someone else is hurt, but that the self—as a rational, social, and meaning-making being—is degraded. To say “I can do what I want with my own life” is to forget that the “I” who wants is the same “I” who is responsible for preserving the capacity to want well. In the end, the duty to oneself is not a burden but a recognition of one’s own dignity. To harm oneself is to deny that dignity, and that is a moral failure—not because of others, but because of what we are.
